expectedText:
TIP POOLING AND GRATUITIES OWNERSHIP — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

ABOUT THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This is an informational sheet about California Labor Code §§ 350-356 — the statutes governing gratuities (tips) paid by patrons to employees of a business, prepared in connection with Acme, Inc. and Jordan Lee.

This document explains, using the statutes' own text, what California law says about who owns a gratuity, what an employer or its agents may and may not do with a gratuity, an employer's record-keeping duty for gratuities received, and the timing rule for gratuities patrons pay by credit card. It is informational only. It does not describe Acme, Inc.'s own tip-pooling or service-charge policies, does not determine how any particular payment, charge, or pooling arrangement should be classified or handled, and is not a substitute for advice from a qualified attorney.

WHAT COUNTS AS A GRATUITY, AND WHO OWNS IT
Under California law, a "gratuity" is any tip, gratuity, money, or part of one, that a patron has paid, given, or left for an employee over and above the actual amount the patron owes the business for the services, goods, food, drink, or articles provided. Every gratuity is the sole property of the employee, or employees, to whom it was paid, given, or left.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "“Gratuity” includes any tip, gratuity, money, or part thereof that has been paid or given to or left for an employee by a patron of a business over and above the actual amount due the business for services rendered or for goods, food, drink, or articles sold or served to the patron."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 350(e), Labor Code, Division 2, Part 1, Chapter 3, Article 1 (Gratuities), definitions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=350.&lawCode=LAB)
  "Every gratuity is hereby declared to be the sole property of the employee or employees to whom it was paid, given, or left for."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 351(a), Labor Code, Division 2, Part 1, Chapter 3, Article 1 (Gratuities), sole property of the employee (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=351.&lawCode=LAB)
  Known gap: This clause covers only the statutory definition in Labor Code § 350(e) and the ownership declaration in § 351(a); it does not address how a specific charge on a specific bill should be classified. The definition's own "over and above the actual amount due the business" language is the statutory hook courts have used to distinguish a voluntary gratuity from a charge that is part of what a patron owes the business (such as certain mandatory service charges) — but this document does not independently verify any case law applying that distinction, for the reason disclosed in the pooling/service-charge clause below.

EMPLOYER AND AGENT MAY NOT TAKE A GRATUITY
No employer or agent may collect, take, or receive any gratuity, or part of one, paid, given to, or left for an employee by a patron. An employer may not deduct any amount from wages due an employee on account of a gratuity, and may not require an employee to credit a gratuity, or part of one, against the wages the employer owes that employee. The Labor Commissioner may investigate and issue a citation, or file a civil action, for a gratuity taken or withheld in violation of this rule.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "No employer or agent shall collect, take, or receive any gratuity or a part thereof that is paid, given to, or left for an employee by a patron, or deduct any amount from wages due an employee on account of a gratuity, or require an employee to credit the amount, or any part thereof, of a gratuity against and as a part of the wages due the employee from the employer."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 351(a), Labor Code, Division 2, Part 1, Chapter 3, Article 1 (Gratuities), prohibition on employer/agent taking gratuities (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=351.&lawCode=LAB)
  "The Labor Commissioner may investigate and issue a citation or file a civil action for gratuities taken or withheld in violation of this section."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 351(b), Labor Code, Division 2, Part 1, Chapter 3, Article 1 (Gratuities), Labor Commissioner enforcement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=351.&lawCode=LAB)
  Known gap: This clause states the general prohibition in Labor Code § 351(a)-(b). It does not address the statute's separate, non-managerial mandatory tip-pooling practice, which is discussed in the pooling/service-charge clause below along with the honest limitation on this session's case-law research. "Agent" is a defined term (§ 350(d)): every person other than the employer who has authority to hire or discharge, or to supervise, direct, or control, employees — this document does not independently determine which specific job titles or roles at any particular business meet that definition.

CREDIT-CARD GRATUITIES: NO FEE DEDUCTION, AND PAYMENT TIMING
When an employer permits patrons to pay gratuities by credit card, the employer must pay employees the full amount of the gratuity the patron indicated on the credit card slip, with no deduction for any credit card payment processing fee or cost the credit card company charges the employer. A gratuity a patron pays by credit card must be paid to the employee no later than the next regular payday following the date the patron authorized the credit card payment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "An employer that permits patrons to pay gratuities by credit card shall pay the employees the full amount of the gratuity that the patron indicated on the credit card slip, without any deductions for any credit card payment processing fees or costs that may be charged to the employer by the credit card company. Payment of gratuities made by patrons using credit cards shall be made to the employees not later than the next regular payday following the date the patron authorized the credit card payment."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 351(a), Labor Code, Division 2, Part 1, Chapter 3, Article 1 (Gratuities), credit-card gratuities (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=351.&lawCode=LAB)
  Known gap: This rule is codified in Labor Code § 351(a) (as currently amended), not in § 356 — a research task describing this timing rule as located in § 356 does not match the current statutory text; § 356 is instead the article's legislative purpose declaration, covered in the enforcement/penalties clause below. This clause does not address gratuities paid by other electronic or app-based payment methods that are not, by their terms, a "credit card," and does not independently verify whether any additional or different timing rule applies to those methods.

EMPLOYER RECORD-KEEPING FOR GRATUITIES
An employer must keep accurate records of all gratuities it receives, whether received directly or indirectly through a deduction from an employee's wages or otherwise. Those records must be open to inspection at all reasonable hours by the Department of Industrial Relations.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Every employer shall keep accurate records of all gratuities received by him, whether received directly from the employee or indirectly by means of deductions from the wages of the employee or otherwise. Such records shall be open to inspection at all reasonable hours by the department."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 353, Labor Code, Division 2, Part 1, Chapter 3, Article 1 (Gratuities), employer record-keeping (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=353.&lawCode=LAB)
  Known gap: Section 353's text is general — it requires accurate records of gratuities "received," without a separate itemized-statement mechanism or credit-card-specific record format; this document does not treat § 353 as imposing a credit-card-specific paperwork requirement distinct from the general recording duty, since the current statutory text does not draw that distinction. This section has not been substantively amended since its original 1937 enactment, so it predates the credit-card gratuity provisions now found in § 351(a).

MANDATORY TIP POOLING AND SERVICE CHARGES: WHAT THE STATUTE DOES AND DOES NOT SAY
The text of Labor Code §§ 350-356 does not itself use the phrase "tip pooling," does not itself list which categories of employee may or may not share in a pooled gratuity, and does not itself define "service charge" as a term separate from "gratuity." The statute's definition of "gratuity" is limited to an amount paid over and above the actual amount a patron owes the business for services, goods, food, drink, or articles — a boundary that bears on whether a particular charge added to a patron's bill is, or is not, a "gratuity" within the statute's own terms.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "“Gratuity” includes any tip, gratuity, money, or part thereof that has been paid or given to or left for an employee by a patron of a business over and above the actual amount due the business for services rendered or for goods, food, drink, or articles sold or served to the patron."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 350(e), Labor Code, Division 2, Part 1, Chapter 3, Article 1 (Gratuities), definition of gratuity (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=350.&lawCode=LAB)
  Known gap: This is a genuine and important gap, not a stylistic choice: California courts have developed real, substantial case law addressing which non-managerial employees may be required to share in a mandatory tip pool, and addressing when a mandatory service charge is or is not treated as a "gratuity" under this article — but this session's CourtListener access was rate-limited ("Rate limit exceeded: 125/day") on the very first lightweight search call made for this topic, before any case could be retrieved, with the daily quota not resetting for roughly 5-6 more hours. Rather than wait out the reset or state a case-law rule from memory without verifying it against the actual opinion text, this document proceeds on the statute's text alone and discloses that choice here. Anyone relying on this document should treat the case-law gloss on tip pooling and service charges as an unverified, separate body of law that this document does not state.

PURPOSE, ENFORCEMENT, AND CRIMINAL PENALTY
The Legislature has declared that this article's purpose is to prevent fraud on the public in connection with tipping, that the article is passed for a public reason, and that it cannot be overridden by a private agreement. The Department of Industrial Relations enforces the article, and any fines collected under it are paid into the state treasury's general fund. Separately, an employer who violates any provision of this article is guilty of a misdemeanor, punishable by a fine of not more than one thousand dollars ($1,000), imprisonment of not more than 60 days, or both.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The Legislature expressly declares that the purpose of this article is to prevent fraud upon the public in connection with the practice of tipping and declares that this article is passed for a public reason and can not be contravened by a private agreement."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 356, Labor Code, Division 2, Part 1, Chapter 3, Article 1 (Gratuities), legislative purpose declaration (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=356.&lawCode=LAB)
  "The Department of Industrial Relations shall enforce the provisions of this article. All fines collected under this article shall be paid into the State treasury and credited to the general fund."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 355, Labor Code, Division 2, Part 1, Chapter 3, Article 1 (Gratuities), agency enforcement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=355.&lawCode=LAB)
  "Any employer who violates any provision of this article is guilty of a misdemeanor, punishable by a fine not exceeding one thousand dollars ($1,000) or by imprisonment for not exceeding 60 days, or both."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 354, Labor Code, Division 2, Part 1, Chapter 3, Article 1 (Gratuities), misdemeanor penalty (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=354.&lawCode=LAB)
  Known gap: Sections 354, 355, and 356 are three separate statutory sections, treated here together because each addresses enforcement or the article's binding, non-waivable character rather than a substantive tipping rule. This document does not independently verify how often, or under what circumstances, the misdemeanor penalty in § 354 has actually been charged or prosecuted, and does not address civil remedies (such as those available through the Labor Commissioner under § 351(b) or through a private civil action) beyond what those other clauses already state.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT OF RECEIPT
Jordan Lee acknowledges receiving this informational sheet about California Labor Code §§ 350-356 governing gratuities. This acknowledgment confirms only that Jordan Lee received and reviewed this sheet. It does not describe, approve, or waive any right or defense regarding any tip-pooling arrangement, service charge, or gratuity-handling practice of Acme, Inc.

Employee: Jordan Lee
Date: September 1, 2026
Oakland, California
